newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Fraser to close stores, losses deepen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Fraser to close stores, losses deepen.

text.p: House of Fraser, the loss-making British department store chain, sank deeper into the red on Tuesday and announced a swingeing cost-cutting drive that could bring hundreds of job cuts and up to 10 store closures.
The company, beset by problems since its flotation in 1994, said new management efforts to revive the business would start to show through next year.
But investors remained sceptical about the recovery programme and the group's shares fell 6.5 pence to 156 pence, well down on the flotation price in April 1994 of 180 pence.
The group's loss before tax and and exceptional costs widened to 13.6 million pounds ($21.29 million) from 4.3 million. Sales rose to 334.7 million pounds from 322.6 million.
The dividend was held at 1.7 pence a share.

Finance director Richard Scott estimated it would need to make provisions of between 40 and 50 million pounds in its full year accounts to pay for possible store closures, job cuts and the write-down of unwanted stock.
"On the very prudent side at this stage it's probabably going to be between 40 and 50 million...It's a very conservative figure," finance director Richard Scott told Reuters in a telephone interview.
The group is also looking to save money by reducing head office costs and introducing a cheaper refurbishment programme for stores it plans to keep.
Chief executive John Coleman said the group's market share had been eroded and poor sales of "own bought" fashions, particularly women's, could not support the high cost base.
He told a news conference the company would strip out surplus costs, sell off unwanted stock and close or ditch stores which would be unprofitable over the long term.
But he declined to say which of its 51 stores might be shut or how many jobs could go. There had been speculation that as many as 1,000 jobs could go, but he would not discuss actual numbers.

Coleman, who replaced Andrew Jennings as chief executive in April, said mismanagement led to stock problems and was also to blame for the sales slump in high margin "own bought" womenswear, which includes own-label as well as branded goods.
Shoppers bought instead from concessions in the stores -- such as Alexon and Windsmoor -- which saw a 29 percent jump in womenswear sales.
"We've been a failure across the board (in womenswear), Coleman said.

The group hopes new management can reverse the trend by using market research which has identified the typical House of Fraser shopper as career women, younger fashion lovers and more mature women who want quality, classic clothes.

Scott said the concessions operating within House of Fraser had scored successes with classic clothing. But the group's own ranges had done poorly because they were pitched to compete with Marks and Spencer and that had proved difficult.
"Own bought" menswear fared better with sales up by 21 percent. But in total concessions accounted for more than a third of total sales.
